newsitem.title: USA: Sales of new homes unexpectedly strong in May.
newsitem.headline: Sales of new homes unexpectedly strong in May.

text.p: Sales of new homes were unexpectedly strong in May, the Commerce Department said on Monday, jumping at the strongest rate in six months.

Sales climbed 7.1 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 825,000 units -- well above Wall Street economists' expectations of a 786,000-unit rate -- after a revised 8.1 percent fall in April. It was the strongest pickup in monthly sales since an 11.6 percent increase last November and brought the supply of new homes on the market down to its lowest in nearly 26 years.

A steadily expanding economy has bolstered consumer confidence and fattened incomes by creating tens of thousands of jobs that have enabled existing homeowners to trade up to larger homes or to enter the market for the first time.
That was reflected in the low 4.1 months' worth of new homes on the market in May. It was the lowest supply since July 1971, when there also was a 4.1-months' worth supply.

Previously, the department said sales fell 7.7 percent in April to a rate of 772,000, but it revised that slightly. The monthly revisions have become smaller since the department changed its collection methods for the monthly sales data, using laptop computers to get a more accurate count.
Mortgage rates have remained remarkably stable, and low by historical standards, despite the economy completing six years of unbroken expansion in March from the last recession in 1990-91.

The Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. said rates for a 30-year mortgage loan averaged 7.94 percent in May, barely up from 7.92 percent in April. But they were still lower than the 8.07 percent mortgage rate available a year earlier, in May 1996.

Federal Reserve policy-makers meet on Tuesday and Wednesday to plot interest-rate strategy. The Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to keep rates unchanged, a further help to the housing sector.
Last week, the National Association of Realtors said sales of existing, or used, homes also rose 4.4 percent in May to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.24 million.

For new homes, the May sales jump was especially evident in the Midwest, where they soared 23.9 percent to 166,000, the strongest rise since a 31.7 percent jump in January 1996. It was the strongest monthly increase in Midwestern sales since a 31.7 percent increase in January 1996, the department said.
In the Northeast, sales rose 15.1 percent in May to 107,000 and in the South they were up 5.3 percent to 357,000.
The only region where sales fell during May was in the West, where they were down 4.4 percent to 195,000.
The average home sales price in May fell to $166,900 from $179,700 in April, while the median sales price was down to $139,900 from $150,000.
